judgment.rationale: Both are Class-4 Content bullets (rank 3) under Competency C-5.1 ('Collects data... represents it in tabular form and as pictograph, bar graphs and interprets it'). The first, 'Learns to record data' (LC: 'Record data'), is the recording step of the data-handling sequence; the second extends this to representation and cross-representation reasoning ('Depict data in the form of a table', 'Depict data in the form of a pictograph', 'Relate data shown in a pictograph and in a table'). Depicting recorded data in tables/pictographs and relating the two representations presupposes the ability to record data, so proficiency in the first substantively supports success in the second despite equal class rank; this is pair-specific extension rather than generic repetition. Shared parentage and the 'data' token overlap alone were not treated as sufficient. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so the excerpt-based reading is bounded.

judgment.rationale: Both are Class-1 Content SFIs (same canonical rank 0) under CG-1 but different competencies: the first (C-1.9) is comparing and ordering objects by length, weight and capacity using comparative pairs (long-short, heavy-light, more-less, most-least), while the second (C-1.10) is 'Long and short time activities', whose LC is 'compare everyday activities to tell which takes a long time and which takes a short time'. They share the same comparative-language reasoning applied to different attributes (physical magnitude versus duration), giving substantive conceptual coherence and mutual reinforcement of comparison vocabulary. Evidence does not substantiate a same-rank developmental dependency in either direction: neither statement extends, combines, or increases complexity relative to the other, and the overlap ('compare', 'more', 'less', 'long', 'short') is largely vocabulary-level plus same-page proximity. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment; note both endpoints' source evidence and the first endpoint's LC evidence are truncated and nomination evidence is truncated, though the retained text is sufficient for this symmetric reading.

judgment.rationale: First (Class-5, C-2.3) is computational: division of three- and four-digit numbers by one- and two-digit divisors, with LCs naming each division case. Second (Class-4, C-2.4) is applied: solving money/price-list problems using the four basic operations, with LCs for addition, subtraction, multiplication and division in a money context. They share the CG-2 four-operations goal and both involve division, so there is genuine conceptual coherence between applying operations in money transactions and developing multi-digit division facility. However, the Class-4 money statement does not specify computational demand (divisor/dividend size) and sits under a different competency (money transactions), so the evidence does not show that proficiency in money problem solving substantively supports success in multi-digit division algorithms; the likelier support runs the other way, which is not a permitted direction. Symmetric relatesTo therefore fits better than the permitted second_to_first buildsTowards. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, limiting detail on computational range.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content SFIs under Competency C-3.1 / CG-3 (attributes of 2D and 3D shapes, spatial description). The first (Class-3, rank 2) is 'Models objects using these shapes' — constructing/representing real objects with 2D and 3D shapes; the second (Class-5, rank 4) is 'Identify angles in things around us using turns' — recognising angle as an amount of turn in everyday objects. They share the geometric-attributes-in-real-objects theme and both apply shape reasoning to the surrounding environment, which is substantive same-competency coherence. However, the Class-5 skill introduces a distinct construct (angle as turn, dynamic rotation) that is not an extension or refinement of modelling with solids and figures; proficiency in modelling objects does not specifically support identifying angles via turns, and the surface nomination overlap is generic ('shapes', 'using', trigram fragments) plus same-page proximity, which alone is not developmental evidence. Therefore symmetric relatesTo rather than buildsTowards. Ancestor competency and curricular goal lack developmental coordinates and both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence, so only bounded excerpt text was used.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content SFIs under Competency C-1.3 ('Groups objects using two or more attributes or properties'). The Class-1 item (rank 0) asks learners to classify objects by observable behaviour features (rolling and sliding); the Class-2 item (rank 1) extends the same classification skill to explicit geometric attributes of solids — flat vs round/curved surfaces, straight vs curved edges, and corners — using named everyday objects, and its LCs decompose into three distinct attribute-based criteria versus the single-criterion Class-1 LC. This is substantive deepening from informal single-feature sorting to multi-attribute geometric classification, so Class-1 proficiency supports success in the Class-2 expectation; direction follows the lower-to-higher class rank.

judgment.rationale: Both are Class-4 Content items (rank 3) under CG-3, but they sit under different competencies: 'Symmetrical shapes through paper folding and mirror' under C-3.3 (recognises and creates symmetry, incl. reflection) and 'Growing patterns using symmetry' under C-3.4 (identifies, describes and extends patterns in shapes).
